title: Find the Power of K-Size Subarrays I
spaceBreakdown:
- int bad, loop indices i: O(1)
- vector<int> res: size n-k+1, returned output (not counted)
- not counted: input nums, returned res
approach: A window of size k is "powerful" iff every adjacent pair inside it increases by exactly 1 (nums[j+1] == nums[j]+1); then it is automatically consecutive and ascending, so its max is the last element nums[i+k-1]. When the window slides one step right, only two adjacent pairs change membership: pair (i-1,i) leaves and pair (i+k-2,i+k-1) enters. So we keep a single integer `bad` = number of bad pairs currently inside the window, updating it by ±1 per slide. Answer is nums[i+k-1] when bad==0, else -1.
hints: When a window of size k slides one step to the right, how many adjacent pairs actually change membership inside it? (n ≤ 500, k ≤ n.)
Use a sliding window with a running counter of "bad" adjacent pairs where nums[j+1] ≠ nums[j]+1. In [1,2,3,4,3,2,5] with k=3, window [3,4,3] contains the bad pair (4,3), so its power is -1.

```
bad = count of pairs (j,j+1) in first window with nums[j+1] != nums[j]+1
res[0] = (bad == 0) ? nums[k-1] : -1
for i = 1 to n-k:
    if nums[i] != nums[i-1]+1: bad--
    if nums[i+k-1] != nums[i+k-2]+1: bad++
    res[i] = (bad == 0) ? nums[i+k-1] : -1
```

**All equal elements** - every adjacent pair fails the +1 test.
`Input: nums = [2,2,2,2,2], k = 4` → `Expected: [-1,-1]`
⚠️ Bug: testing `nums[j+1] >= nums[j]` (non-decreasing) instead of `nums[j+1] == nums[j]+1` → returns `[2,2]`

**Already consecutive ascending** - the whole array is one valid run.
`Input: nums = [1,2,3,4], k = 4` → `Expected: [4]`
⚠️ Bug: returning `nums[i]` (window start) as the max instead of `nums[i+k-1]` → returns `[1]`

**k = 1** - each window is a single element with no adjacent pairs to check.
`Input: nums = [7,3,5], k = 1` → `Expected: [7,3,5]`
⚠️ Bug: treating an empty pair set as invalid (initializing bad = 1) → returns `[-1,-1,-1]`

**Boundary last window** - the final slide must add the last pair correctly.
`Input: nums = [1,2,3,4,5], k = 3` → `Expected: [3,4,5]`
⚠️ Bug: loop condition `i + k < n` instead of `i + k - 1 < n` → skips last window, returns `[3,4]`

followUps.q: If n grows to 10^6, does this approach still hold?
followUps.a: Yes. The algorithm is O(n) time and O(1) extra space, so it scales linearly; only the returned vector grows with n.

followUps.q: What if "consecutive" means differing by a fixed step d (not necessarily 1)?
followUps.a: Replace the bad-pair test `nums[j+1] != nums[j]+1` with `nums[j+1] != nums[j]+d`. The same single-counter sliding window gives O(n) time and O(1) space.

followUps.q: What if you need the power for every subarray size, not just k?
followUps.a: For each index, compute the longest run of good pairs it belongs to; any window of size ≤ run_length+1 starting there is valid with power = its last element. Enumerate runs in O(n) and fill answer ranges, still O(n) time and O(n) output space.
